title: Mitral Stenosis Fish Mouth, Calcific Aortic Stenosis, Mitral Prolapse, and Infective Endocarditis

steps.tx: Chronic rheumatic heart disease is the overwhelming cause of acquired mitral stenosis, resulting from post-inflammatory fibrous scarring following acute rheumatic carditis. Decades of chronic fibrous repair cause extensive fibrous thickening and calcification of valve leaflets, diffuse commissural fusion, and severe shortening and chordal fusion. The resulting rigid, non-compliant, funnel-shaped valve resembles a **fish-mouth mitral orifice**, also termed a buttonhole deformity. The normal valve area (four to six square centimeters) narrows below 1.5 square centimeters, obstructing left ventricular inflow.
steps.say: Rheumatic carditis is the primary cause of chronic mitral stenosis. Over decades, recurrent inflammation and turbulent flow cause the leaflet commissures to fuse together, the leaflets to thicken and calcify, and the chordae tendineae to shorten into dense cords. Viewed from the left atrium, the scarred, immobile valve orifice looks like the gaping mouth of a fish or a buttonhole, severely restricting diastolic inflow into the left ventricle.

vis.alt: Gross anatomical photograph showing the fish-mouth buttonhole deformity of severe rheumatic mitral stenosis
vis.caption: Mitral stenosis pathophysiology with left atrial pressure overload and pulmonary consequences.

steps.tx: Severe mitral stenosis imposes an immense haemodynamic upstream pressure burden. The obstruction to diastolic inflow elevates left atrial pressure, causing progressive left atrial dilatation and hypertrophy. Extreme atrial stretching disrupts the cardiac conduction system, triggering atrial fibrillation in over forty percent of patients. Sluggish, turbulent blood flow within the fibrillating atrial appendage promotes **left atrial mural thrombosis**, posing an extreme risk of systemic arterial embolization and embolic stroke. Upstream pulmonary venous congestion produces chronic passive pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure.
steps.say: The tight mitral orifice prevents blood from entering the left ventricle during diastole, causing left atrial pressure to climb. The left atrium dilates massively, which disrupts conduction pathways and precipitates atrial fibrillation. Stagnant blood in the dilated left atrial appendage readily forms large mural thrombi, making embolic stroke a constant danger. Meanwhile, backward pressure causes pulmonary venous congestion and eventually drives right-sided heart failure.

steps.tx: Calcific aortic stenosis is the most frequent surgical valve lesion in developed nations, presenting in two distinct settings: age-related degenerative wear of a normal trileaflet valve (manifesting in the seventh and eighth decades) or accelerated wear of a **congenitally bicuspid aortic valve** (presenting two decades earlier, in the fifth and sixth decades). Chronic mechanical stress stimulates valvular interstitial cells to undergo osteogenic differentiation. Heaped-up nodular calcified masses of hydroxyapatite deposit within the non-coronary and coronary sinuses of Valsalva, projecting into the lumen without commissural fusion.
steps.say: Calcific aortic stenosis is the most common reason for aortic valve replacement. In patients with normal trileaflet valves, it develops from wear-and-tear in their seventies and eighties. In individuals born with a bicuspid aortic valve, abnormal mechanical shear accelerates calcification, causing severe stenosis twenty years earlier. Valvular interstitial cells transform into osteoblast-like cells, depositing rocky mounds of calcium within the sinuses of Valsalva without commissural fusion.

left.title: Calcific Aortic Stenosis
points: Rocky, heaped-up calcium nodules in sinuses of Valsalva
Leaflet commissures remain completely free and unfused
Normal or bicuspid congenital architecture
Affects elderly individuals (70s-80s) or bicuspid (50s-60s)

right.title: Rheumatic Aortic Stenosis
points: Prominent fibrous fusion of leaflet commissures
Coexists with rheumatic mitral valve involvement in >95%
Leaflet edges scarred, thickened, and retracted
Accompanied by post-inflammatory neovascularization

steps.tx: Mitral valve prolapse, also known as Barlow disease, affects two to three percent of the population. The primary anatomical lesion is **myxomatous leaflet degeneration**, characterized by marked expansion of the middle proteoglycan-rich spongiosa layer and concomitant attenuation of the structural fibrosa layer. The accumulation of loose, basophilic dermatan sulfate ground substance softens the valve tissue. During ventricular systole, the redundant, rubbery leaflet scallops billow or parachute retrogradely into the left atrium, producing a classic mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur.
steps.say: Mitral valve prolapse occurs when the structural core of the mitral leaflets undergoes myxomatous degeneration. The central spongiosa layer expands with basophilic glycosaminoglycans while the fibrous backbone weakens. This leaves the leaflets rubbery, enlarged, and loose. During systole, high left ventricular pressure pushes the billowing leaflets backwards into the left atrium like parachutes, creating a characteristic mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur.

vis.alt: Micrograph of myxomatous mitral valve prolapse showing expanded, loose basophilic spongiosa layer and attenuated fibrosa
vis.caption: Mitral valve prolapse pathology with myxomatous leaflet billowing.

steps.tx: Although the vast majority of patients with mitral valve prolapse pursue a completely benign, asymptomatic clinical course, a small subset develops serious cardiovascular sequelae. Progressive leaflet stretching and chordal elongation predispose to spontaneous **chordae tendineae rupture**, precipitating acute, severe mitral regurgitation and congestive pulmonary edema. Furthermore, the constant mechanical trauma and endothelial microabrasions on billowing leaflet surfaces create a prime substrate for platelet-fibrin thrombus deposition, predisposing to transient ischemic attacks, ventricular arrhythmias, and secondary infective endocarditis.
steps.say: While most people with mitral valve prolapse live normal lives, serious complications can occur. As chordae tendineae stretch over years, they can suddenly snap, causing acute mitral regurgitation and pulmonary edema. The constant chafing of billowing leaflets also damages their endothelial lining, predisposing patients to bacterial seeding and infective endocarditis, or acting as a nidus for microthrombi that embolize to the brain.

left.title: Benign Mitral Prolapse Course
points: Asymptomatic mid-systolic click on routine exam
Normal left ventricular dimensions and ejection fraction
Trace or mild physiological mitral regurgitation
Requires reassurance and periodic clinical follow-up

right.title: Severe Complicated Prolapse
points: Spontaneous rupture of thinned chordae tendineae
Acute severe mitral regurgitation with pulmonary edema
Substrate for bacterial colonization in infective endocarditis
Requires surgical mitral valve repair or annuloplasty

steps.tx: The multi-step pathogenesis of infective endocarditis requires two concurrent pathophysiological events: endothelial surface disruption and transient bacteremia. Valvular endothelial damage caused by turbulent flow or catheters exposes subendothelial collagen, triggering platelet-fibrin deposition to form a sterile, non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis nidus. When transient bacteremia occurs (following dental manipulation, intravenous drug use, or genitourinary instrumentation), circulating microorganisms adhere to the platelet-fibrin meshwork via bacterial surface adhesins, rapidly multiplying and synthesizing **destructive septic vegetations** that erode underlying leaflet collagen.
steps.say: Infective endocarditis develops through a two-step mechanism. First, turbulent blood flow damages valve endothelium, prompting platelets and fibrin to form a sterile clot called non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis. Second, transient bacteremia occurs from brushing teeth, dental work, or intravenous injections. Bacteria adhere to the sticky platelet-fibrin clot using surface adhesins, proliferating within the protective matrix and releasing enzymes that destroy valve tissue.

rows: Creates sterile hemostatic nidus on leaflet

steps.tx: Infective endocarditis presents clinically across two classical patterns: acute and subacute forms. **Acute infective endocarditis** is classically caused by virulent pathogens, predominantly Staphylococcus aureus, attacking previously normal heart valves. It produces rapid, fulminant destruction with leaflet perforation, annular ring abscesses, severe acute valvular regurgitation, high remittent fever, and high mortality. Conversely, subacute infective endocarditis is caused by low-virulence oral commensals, primarily Streptococcus viridans, colonizing previously damaged, scarred, or prosthetic valves, pursuing an insidious, protracted febrile course over months.
steps.say: Infective endocarditis presents in acute and subacute clinical varieties. Acute endocarditis is driven by highly virulent bacteria like Staphylococcus aureus attacking previously normal valves. It rapidly chews through valve leaflets and valve rings, causing acute heart failure, septic shock, and death within days. In contrast, subacute endocarditis is caused by low-virulence organisms like Streptococcus viridans attacking previously scarred valves, causing low-grade fevers and night sweats over months.

left.title: Acute Infective Endocarditis
points: Pathogen: Highly virulent Staphylococcus aureus
Target: Frequently strikes normal heart valves
Pathology: Rapid leaflet perforation, annular abscesses
Clinical tempo: Fulminant course, fatal in days without surgery

right.title: Subacute Infective Endocarditis
points: Pathogen: Low-virulence Streptococcus viridans
Target: Prior abnormal valves (rheumatic, bicuspid, prolapse)
Pathology: Bulky, less invasive vegetations, granulation tissue
Clinical tempo: Indolent fever, anemia, weight loss over months

steps.tx: The systemic peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis are generated by two distinct pathological processes: septic microembolization and circulating immune complex vasculitis. Septic microemboli dislodging from friable vegetations produce non-tender, erythematous, haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles termed **Janeway lesions**, alongside linear splinter haemorrhages beneath nail beds. In contrast, circulating antigen-antibody complexes deposit in microvessels, activating complement to produce exquisitely painful, nodular erythematous swellings on the pads of fingers and toes termed Osler nodes, oval retinal hemorrhages with pale centers (Roth spots), and glomerulonephritis.
steps.say: The classic peripheral signs of endocarditis arise through two different mechanisms: septic emboli and immune complex deposition. Janeway lesions are flat, non-tender red spots on the palms and soles caused by septic microemboli lodging in dermal capillaries. In contrast, Osler nodes are raised, intensely painful nodules on the fingertips caused by immune complexes triggering local vasculitis. Immune complexes also deposit in the eyes to produce Roth spots and in the kidneys to cause focal glomerulonephritis.

quiz.q: What morphological feature characterizes the mitral valve in severe chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis?
options: Commissural fusion, chordal shortening, and fish-mouth buttonhole deformity
Heaped-up calcific nodules in the sinuses of Valsalva without commissural fusion
Myxomatous expansion of the spongiosa layer with leaflet billowing into the left atrium
Sterile, non-destructive bland vegetations distributed loosely along lines of closure
quiz.explain: Chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis is defined by leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening, creating a rigid funnel-shaped fish-mouth or buttonhole orifice.

quiz.q: What pathogenic mechanism produces Janeway lesions on the palms and soles in infective endocarditis?
options: Septic microembolization from vegetations producing localized dermal microabscesses
Deposition of circulating immune complexes in dermal post-capillary venules
Severe systemic thrombocytopenia causing non-inflammatory petechial extravasation
Hypersensitivity reaction to empiric beta-lactam antibiotic therapy
quiz.explain: Janeway lesions are non-tender erythematous macules on the palms and soles caused by septic microemboli from friable endocarditic vegetations.

quiz.q: What is the primary histological defect in mitral valve prolapse (Barlow disease)?
options: Expansion of the glycosaminoglycan-rich spongiosa layer with attenuation of the fibrosa
Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with rich plasma cell infiltrates
Diffuse dystrophic calcification starting at the commissures and extending to the annulus
Granulomatous Aschoff body formation within the substance of the valve cusps
quiz.explain: Mitral valve prolapse is caused by myxomatous degeneration: the central proteoglycan-rich spongiosa expands while the fibrous structural core (fibrosa) thins, causing leaflet billowing.
